query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: An integrated approach that combines high‐throughput CALPHAD extrapolations, first-principles–informed MD simulations (using, e.g., 2NN MEAM potentials), and targeted differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) measurements can yield accurate determinations of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, melting-induced volume change, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across single‐phase high-entropy alloys with equiatomic or near-equiatomic compositions. This methodology leverages chemical short-range order to guide the phase energetics during melting.
generation.material_initial_state: Single‐phase high-entropy alloys (e.g., FCC or BCC structured equiatomic alloys) in both single-crystal and polycrystalline forms.
generation.intervention: Apply a computational protocol in which CALPHAD and MD simulations predict phase energetics and structural rearrangements during heating, which is then calibrated with DSC experiments measuring temperature-dependent heat capacity and endothermic/exothermic transitions.
generation.conditions: Heating the sample under controlled atmospheres (e.g., inert gas), with incremental temperature steps from room temperature to above the melting point; simulations are conducted at comparable temperature ranges and relaxation times to capture pre-melting phenomena.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical ordering (including short-range order and grain-boundary effects) that governs the onset of atomic rearrangements during melting, as well as the liquid-state mixing behavior.
generation.mechanism: The method leverages the physical rationale that high configurational entropy and specific local ordering in HEAs lead to predictable enthalpic and volumetric changes near melting. MD simulation captures atomic-scale diffusion and phase change processes (including grain-boundary pre-melting), while CALPHAD models extrapolate known binary/ternary interactions across multicomponent systems. DSC measurements provide direct measurement of thermal properties to calibrate and validate simulation predictions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The combined approach is expected to predict melting temperatures within an error margin of about ±5%, fusion enthalpy and entropy with errors around ±10%, and correct trends in volume changes at melting. Liquid-phase thermodynamic properties (such as non-ideal mixing behavior) are expected to follow predictions from the computed excess free energies and be consistent with in-situ imaging evidence.
generation.baseline: Conventional DSC measurements and direct structural imaging (e.g., neutron or synchrotron X-ray imaging) on well-characterized single-crystal or large-grain HEA samples.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be valid for single-phase, equiatomic or near-equiatomic HEAs with relatively simple phase behavior. It might be less applicable in cases where pronounced phase separation, intermetallic compound formation, or amorphization occurs due to extreme compositional fluctuations or non-ideal mixing in either solid or liquid state.
generation.uncertainty: While the integration of computational and experimental techniques is promising, uncertainties remain regarding the precise error margins for systems with strong local chemical clustering or significant grain-boundary contributions. There is also uncertainty in applying the method to non-equiatomic or multiphase alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a statistically significant set of equiatomic high-entropy alloy samples (covering FCC and BCC structures), then perform high-resolution DSC measurements (with simultaneous dilatometry or in-situ diffraction) to measure melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and volume change at melting. Independently, carry out CALPHAD/MD predictions using the proposed integrated protocol. Compare the predicted properties with the directly measured values.
measurements: Melting temperature (via DSC and in-situ imaging/diffraction)
Fusion enthalpy and entropy (via integrated DSC analysis)
Volume change at melting (via thermal dilatometry or high-temperature XRD)
Liquid-phase behavior (via neutron imaging or synchrotron studies)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the integrated approach fails to predict the measured melting temperature within ±5% or the fusion enthalpy/entropy and volume change within ±10% error consistently across the sample set, or if key trends predicted (e.g., effect of grain-boundary pre-melting) are not observed experimentally, then the proposed methodology would be considered falsified.

AbstractWe determined the entropy of high entropy alloys by investigating single-crystalline nickel and five high entropy alloys: two fcc-alloys, two bcc-alloys and one hcp-alloy. Since the configurational entropy of these single-phase alloys differs from alloys using a base element, it is important to quantify the entropy. Using differential scanning calorimetry, cp-measurements are carried out from −170 °C to the materials’ solidus temperatures TS. From these experiments, we determined the thermal entropy and compared it to the configurational entropy for each of the studied alloys. We applied the rule of mixture to predict molar heat capacities of the alloys at room temperature, which were in good agreement with the Dulong-Petit law. The molar heat capacity of the studied alloys was about three times the universal gas constant, hence the thermal entropy was the major contribution to total entropy. The configurational entropy, due to the chemical composition and number of components, contributes less on the absolute scale. This study employs the MD simulation using 2NN MEAM potential to investigate the melting mechanism and the short-ranged order change for the single crystal and polycrystalline Nb20.6Mo21.7Ta15.6W21.1V21.0 RHEAs with the average grain sizes of 5.2, 10.0, 15.6, 20.1, and 25.3 nm. The MaxEnt theory was used to build the structures for all Nb20.6Mo21.7Ta15.6W21.1V21.0 RHEAs. For polycrystalline Nb20.6Mo21.7Ta15.6W21.1V21.0 RHEAs, the GB atom fraction increases parabolically from 6.2 to 26.8% when the average grain size decreases from 25.3 to 5.2 nm. At 300 K, short-ranged order values of the same element type pairs are larger than 0.8, indicating that all element types are arranged in the most uniform distribution. For pairs of different element types, all short-ranged order values are smaller than − 0.1, indicating that the affinity of these pairs is much higher than those with the same element types.
